```{r}
#Part A
m1 <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
m1

m2 <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
m2

scores <- matrix(c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84, 90), nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
rownames(scores) <- c("Quiz1", "Quiz2")
colnames(scores) <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid")
scores

#Question 1
# byrow = TRUE changes how R fills a matrix. By default, R fills the matrix by column, going from top to bottom. Then it fiils it my left to right. This makes m1 and m2 look different even though it's the same.

#Question 2
matrix(1:8, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
#It showed a warning but still filled in a number in the missing row and column.
```

```{r}
#Part B
scores <- matrix(c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84, 90), nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
rownames(scores) <- c("Quiz1", "Quiz2")
colnames(scores) <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid")

scores[1, 2]

scores[1,]

scores[, "Ben"]

scores[scores >= 90]

#Question 3
class(scores[1, ])
class(scores[, "Ben"])
#Both results are downgraded to a vector, with the class "numeric". R does this automatically because a single row or column contains only one dimension of values. The result to the simplest suitable data structure instead of keeping it as a matrix.

#Question 4
#The value that satisfy the condition and coverts them into a one-demensional vector. This loses the original matrix shape and row/column names because the result is no longer treated as a matrix. scores[1, ] selects a specific row and can retain its column names becuase it subsets the matrix with its position.
```

```{r}
#Part C
dim(scores)
nrow(scores)
ncol(scores)

scores_t <- t(scores)
scores_t
dim(scores_t)
dim(scores)

a <- matrix(1:4, nrow = 2)
b <- matrix(5:8, nrow = 2)
a + b
a * b
a %*% b

#Question 5
#(a * b) multiplies each element of a by b on the same position. (a %*% b) multiplies each row of the first matrix by each column of the second matrix and adds the products together to produce each result.

#Question 6
# Its rows become columns and its columns become rows. The row and column names must also swap position to stay attached to the same data.
```

```{r}
#Part D
scores_v2 <- cbind(scores, Dex = c(85, 91))
scores_v2

scores_v3 <- rbind(scores, Quiz3 = c(80, 88, 93))
scores_v3

#Question 7
cbind(scores, c(85, 91, 100))

#Question 8
#rbind() when adding new observations as rows to a dataset over time. In a daily sales dataset, I would use rbind() to add a new row containing the sales figures for each new day. 
```

```{r}
#Part E
arr <- array(1:12, dim = c(2, 3, 2))
arr

arr[1, 2, 2]

arr[, , 1]

dim(arr)

#Question 9
#Three numbers returned by dim(arr) represent the array's dimensions. First number, 2 represents the rows; second number, 3 the columns. 2 represent the layers or slices. Therefore, the array contains two 2-by-3 matrics.

#Question 10
#Real-world exapmle will be school's exam scores recorded across multiple quizzes.
```

```{r}
#Part F
all_students <- rbind(class_a, class_b)
all_students

rowMeans(all_students)

#Question 11
#I chose rbind() because the two matrics represent different students with the same columns, Midterm and Final. While cbind() would add new columns

#Question 12
#I would combine the five class matircs using rbind() so that the students from all classes are placed into one matrix.
```
#Conclusion
#A matrix is a two-dimensional data structure with rows and columns, while an array can have three or more dimensions. Matrices are useful for organizing data such as student scores, while arrays can store additional dimensions such as exam dates. The rbind() function adds new rows, while cbind() adds new columns. For example, I could use rbind() to add new students to a class score dataset or cbind() to add a new exam score column.nenc
